rationale: A wins because it keeps its ambition inside the facts. "Brex takes its Ramp rivalry global with cards in 50 countries" is a clean competitive angle built from the update; B's "multinational-payroll problem hits mid-size companies" wanders into payroll and mid-market claims the brief never gave it. B is sharper in places, but sharp fiction is still fiction.
gaps_in_A: "Brex spends big on global infrastructure" assumes spending level and infrastructure cost the update does not disclose.
"CFOs of global startups" is plausible, but the update gives enterprise customer demand and venture-backed customers, not CFO sources or a startup-specific request.
"domestic-first B2B tools can't stay domestic" is a defensible thesis only after outside pattern proof; from the supplied facts alone, it is a little overbuilt.
Calling a traditional-issuer angle a "duplicate" may collapse a potentially distinct incumbent-bank lens too early.
gaps_in_B: "multinational-payroll problem hits mid-size companies" invents both payroll and mid-size company framing. The update is about cards, expenses, and reimbursement.
"Brex bets 50 countries is the thing Ramp can't copy quickly" asserts Ramp weakness without evidence. That is the sort of line a competitor turns into a correction.
"after years of fighting over the same US venture-backed customer base" adds history and geography not supplied in the brief.
"every Series B a multi-country employer" and "FX-mangled reimbursements" sound vivid, but they are invented customer pain without a named customer or data.
